replying_to: Replying to Learning Representations of Partial Subgraphs by Subgraph InfoMax
display_title: Official Review of Paper20 by Reviewer 38CS

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper investigates the problem of subgraph classification on a graph, and proposes a subgraph infomax based method to address the representation learning of partial subgraphs. Experiments on three datasets show that the proposed model can outperform the baselines.
content.main_review:
Several main concerns should be well-addressed by the authors.

1. In the Introduction, the authors claim that "Similar to these previous models that maximize MI between the global summary (e.g., graph) and local parts (e.g., nodes)". Actually, some of them also consider the MI maximization between nodes and subgraphs. From this point, the novelty of this paper is a bit incremental.


2. 
- (1) Another problem, multi-graph classification, which aims to learn graph-level representations for graph classification, is quite similar to this one, if we change the subgraphs (in this paper) to graphs (in the multi-graph setting). However, no comparison as well as the survey of related studies are given.

- (2) Besides, some recent studies such as [1,2] investigate the MI maximization in the multi-graph setting (though [1] is cited). The proposed model in this paper has a similar setting with these approaches, and they also share similar designs. The authors should comprehensively compare these approaches with the proposed model.


3. The motivation that why the usage of MI maximization can enhance the subgraph classification performance is not clearly presented. The authors should give more details here. Why the two-levels MI maximization can boost the representations of the partial subgraphs?


4. The authors claim that "With only a few observed nodes, a naive summary based on those few do not hold much information of the entire subgraph". So why the proposed model can refer to more information than those?


5. Some parts of the proposed model are confusing.

- (1) In the section of "Intra-Subgraph InfoMax", the authors claim that "we cannot know the exact boundary of the subgraph at this stage". Why cannot know? In the following part of this paragraph, V^{sub} is utilized to decide the set of V^{sub_k} and V^{glob_k}.

- (2) Why use the k-hop neighbors to select the positive nodes, and is this method definitely correct so that they can serve as the positive nodes? Besides, why not directly utilize the employed V^{sub}? And why V^{glob_k} can serve as the negative nodes?

- (3) At the end of section "Intra-Subgraph InfoMax", the authors employ the hop distance to replace the embedding distance of nodes. However, though efficient, there is an important issue here. GNNs usually resort to neighborhood aggregation to calculate the representations of nodes with a few layers (corresponding to a few hops). Thus the similarity of node embeddings actually reflects the similarity between their context information. Two distant nodes with quite similar context, would also have similar representations. Thus, directly using the hop cannot reflect the true distance between nodes.

- (4) In Eq.(7), the top-k indexes are employed for aggregation. Does the selection of top-k indexes cut off the backpropagation?


6. In Experiments, the baselines are not sufficient. Actually, each subgraph can also be regarded as a graph in the setting of multi-graph classification. This kind of method should be compared. Besides, how about the other MI maximization based approaches, can they perform well on this task?


[1] Graph Cross Networks with Vertex Infomax Pooling. NeurIPS 2020

[2] Graph Pooling via Coarsened Graph Infomax. SIGIR 2021
content.summary_of_the_review:
1. Some parts of this paper are confusing and not well-motivated.
2. The experiments are not sufficient.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper20 by Reviewer 38CS

content.title: Response to 38CS
content.comment:
Thank you for your review and feedback. We addressed the concerns on the motivation, novelty, related work surveys, and baseline comparisons in the [general response](https://openreview.net/forum?id=32KyhxmvmO&noteId=hlhZffX2_0t). We provide answers to your individual questions below.

> The authors claim that "With only a few observed nodes, a naive summary based on those few do not hold much information of the entire subgraph". So why the proposed model can refer to more information than those?

This is because we use two-level MI maximization losses with the subgraph reconstruction. Recall that Inter-SGI assembles nodes of high MI with the observed subgraph using results of Intra-SGI, and reconstructs the subgraph with high MI nodes. Using the reconstructed subgraph allows Inter-SGI to obtain a summary close to the full subgraph under insufficient observation. We elaborate on that section in the revised paper. 

> In the section of "Intra-Subgraph InfoMax", the authors claim that "we cannot know the exact boundary of the subgraph at this stage". Why cannot know? In the following part of this paragraph, V^{sub} is utilized to decide the set of V^{sub_k} and V^{glob_k}.

In the partial subgraph learning problem, the model only knows which nodes are included in the observed subgraph during the forward pass of the inference but does not know which nodes are in the full subgraph. For instance, in the fake news early detection problem, the model at time $t$ does not know which user propagates the news at time $t+1$.

Knowing what $\mathbb{V}^{\text{sub}}$ is and using it can be done only at the training stage. Like labels can be used in the training stage of supervised learning, contrastive learning can know what positive/negative samples are at this stage. We revise the paper to make this clear. 

> Why use the k-hop neighbors to select the positive nodes, and is this method definitely correct so that they can serve as the positive nodes? Besides, why not directly utilize the employed V^{sub}? And why V^{glob_k} can serve as the negative nodes?

We can design models directly employing $\mathbb{V}^{\text{sub}}$ as positive nodes. In fact, that is Inter-SGI. We do not simply use $\mathbb{V}^{\text{sub}}$ because we expect to learn local-global contrast from different hierarchies from both types of summaries and negative samples. In addition, we present experimental results that the performance gains from the two are different case-by-case and that models should be designed according to their characteristics.

Now we explain the rationales in the design of positives ($\mathbb{V}^{\text{sub}_k}$) and negatives ($\mathbb{V}^{\text{glob}_k}$) based on k-hop neighbors in Intra-SGI. Both $\mathbb{V}^{\text{sub}_k}$ and $\mathbb{V}^{\text{glob}_k}$ are sets of nodes in the $k$-hop of the observed subgraph, but the former is a set of nodes belonging to the subgraph, the latter is not. In this context, $\mathbb{V}^{\text{sub}_k}$ and $\mathbb{V}^{\text{glob}_k}$ effectively serve as positive and negative samples. The constraint of k-hop neighbors brings two advantages. First, the number of positive nodes to be used for subgraph reconstruction can be significantly reduced compared to the method using all nodes in the global graph. Second, it enables more effective contrastive learning by providing hard negative samples.  

> (4) In Eq.(7), the top-k indexes are employed for aggregation. Does the selection of top-k indexes cut off the backpropagation?

The top-k pooling does not cut off backpropagation. Similar operations have been used in various end-to-end GNN models [1, 2, 3].

[1] Gao, Hongyang, and Shuiwang Ji. "Graph u-nets." international conference on machine learning. PMLR, 2019.

[2] Cangea, Cătălina, et al. "Towards sparse hierarchical graph classifiers." arXiv preprint arXiv:1811.01287 (2018).

[3] Knyazev, Boris, Graham W. Taylor, and Mohamed Amer. "Understanding Attention and Generalization in Graph Neural Networks." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 32 (2019): 4202-4212.

content.title: Response to z3wS
content.comment:
Thank you for your review and efforts. We addressed the concerns on the motivation, novelty, related work surveys, and baseline comparisons in the [general response](https://openreview.net/forum?id=32KyhxmvmO&noteId=hlhZffX2_0t). We provide an answer to your individual question below.

> the datasets used is very limited, even comparing to the original subGNN paper. I think the authors should conduct experiments on more datasets

The original SubGNN proposed four real-world datasets, and we use three datasets, including two from the SubGNN paper (HPO-Metab, EM-User). The other two datasets we have not experimented with are PPI-BP and HPO-Neuro. PPI-BP is too small to train under partial observations. Moreover, HPO-Neuro has similar characteristics to HPO-Metab since they are both human disorder subgraphs in the human phenotype ontology graph. In this respect, we think that our choices in datasets for this work are sufficient.

display_title: Official Review of Paper20 by Reviewer NYN3

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work explores how to learn partial subgraph representation.
content.main_review:
Learning representations with subgraph has gained more and more attention due because of its multiple benefits to deal with large scale graphs. In this work, a new concept namely partial subgraph has been proposed for some special applications like fake news detection. Then authors give a solution based on MI optimization loss for learning the subgraph classification task. However, there are still many concepts that are not explained properly.

Concerns:
1. The definition of partial graph is not properly presented. As a matter of fact, it's very difficult to have a completed view of a given graph. Because of this, the observed graph is already a partial graph. Why do we need to define the concept "partial subgraph"? What is the relation between partial subgraph and observed subgraph? Is the partial subgraph already an observed one or sampled from the completed graph?

2. The motivation behind the solution is not clear. It's difficult to understand why maximizing the MI loss works for learning partial subgraph? Can recent proposed GNN methods not address the challenges?

Minor issue:
1. The symbols to represent the nodes and edges $\mathbb{V}$ or $\mathbb{A}$ can be easily to be confused with the symbol $\mathbb{R}$.

2. There are some grammar errors. For example, the sentences like "But the dynamics and temporiality xxx, there may be xxx." and "As we introduce a new class of tasks, these should be mainly xxx " in Section 2.2.

Thank you for your review and feedback. We addressed the concern on the motivation in the [general response](https://openreview.net/forum?id=32KyhxmvmO&noteId=hlhZffX2_0t). We provide answers to other points in this reply.

The partial subgraph is the partially observed subgraph. Given the (full) subgraph, we get the partial subgraph if we have only partial observations on this. Sorry for this confusion, and we will make it clear in section 2.1.

Thank you for your opinion, but please note that this is the official typeset from the ICLR 2022. This `\mathbb` font is reserved for sets, such as a set of nodes $\mathbb{V}$, a set of edges $\mathbb{A}$, and a set of real numbers $\mathbb{R}$.

content.title: General Response to All Reviewers (Part 1/2)
content.comment:
We thank the reviewers for their efforts in reviewing. We have got the opportunity to improve and develop our work more. However, most reviews are based on misunderstandings, and our contributions are not sufficiently appreciated. We will clarify our contributions and resolve the reviewers’ questions and comments. We hope reviewers reconsider their opinions by reading our responses and the revised paper (which will be uploaded soon).

We first address two issues that multiple reviewers have raised: (1) unclear motivation, (2) a lack of novelty, related work survey, and baseline comparisons. In addition to them, we will post answers to individual questions as a reply at each review.

## Response to unclear motivation

Reviewers `NYN3` and `38CS` raised an issue of unclear motivation.

The motivation of our model is in the hierarchy of data. As we stated in section 3.2, the partial subgraph learning problem has a structural hierarchy from the global graph to full subgraphs and observed subgraphs. The two-level local-global InfoMax method is designed under the assumption that encoding this hierarchy helps learn the representation of the observed subgraph: Intra-SGI maximizes MI between the *observed subgraph* and nodes, and Inter-SGI maximizes MI between the *full (reconstructed) subgraph* and nodes. By doing so, we can encode different local-global contrasts in the representation and confirm it experimentally.

In addition, it has been actively studied recently to learn the representation of many subcomponents of graph-structured data (related work on page 9). However, existing methods are not proposed for the subgraph-level prediction. Accordingly, these models have not proven their effectiveness in our problem, cannot be applied directly by nature, or get suboptimal results. As an example, we experiment with the Deep Graph InfoMax (DGI) model [1] and demonstrate that our model outperforms DGI in the table below. Since the DGI model is designed for the graph-level representation, we modify it for the subgraph-level representation. The input is an individual observed subgraph, and the corresponding negative sample is its corrupted version by shuffling the node indices.

|Model|FNTN|EM-User|HPO-Metab|
|-|-|-|-|
|Subgraph-level DGI|87.5 ± 1.2|72.3 ± 6.2|44.0 ± 1.8|
|Intra-SGI|87.7 ± 1.0|77.4 ± 3.2|43.8 ± 2.3|
|Inter-SGI|87.3 ± 0.0|75.7 ± 3.9|47.1 ± 2.1|
|Intra/Inter-SGI|89.6 ± 2.2|77.0 ± 2.8|44.6 ± 1.6|

content.title: General Response to All Reviewers (Part 2/2)
content.comment:
## Response to a lack of novelty, related work surveys, and baseline comparisons

Reviewers `z3wS` and `38CS` stated a lack of novelty, related work surveys, and baseline comparisons. These reviews call for comparison with two research areas mainly: self-supervised learning models (including MI maximization) and (multi-) graph prediction models.

### Comparing with self-supervised learning models

> `z3wS`: [...] sees improvement when label data is scarce. [...] the novelty of it compared with existing self-supervised learning method is weak, and there is no any comparison with them.

This argument is valid when our model is positioned as a self-supervised learning model with label scarcity. However, **it is not**. We leverage InfoMax losses as auxiliary losses to learn structural hierarchy in the data, not to overcome the label scarcity problem, even though infoMax is commonly employed in self-supervised models. Accordingly, all the experiments we conduct are in full label settings. Direct comparisons with various self-supervised models (including graphCL, GPT-GNN, and MVGRL mentioned by `z3wS`) are out of the scope of this paper.

The reviewer `38CS` also claimed that the novelty is a bit incremental since some existing studies use MI maximization between nodes and subgraphs. However, these do not aim to learn the subgraph representations. As we mentioned in the related work section, they perform either node prediction or graph prediction tasks. We can anticipate that maximizing MIs between subcomponents might be useful for learning subgraph representations, but we cannot directly apply other MI maximization-based approaches without modifications, and they bring suboptimal results (See DGI results in the table above).
 
### Comparing with (multi-) graph prediction models

The reviewer `38CS` said that since all subgraph predictions can be reducible to (multi-) graph predictions, our paper should include the survey and compare these approaches. We would argue that this line of research is beside the point of our study, and containing them leads to an overly broad survey.

Some famous graph-level benchmarks (IMDB, COLLAB) used in [2, 3] (which `38CS` directly refers to) can be considered as this setting; they are ego-networks from collaboration networks of actors and scientists. However, our research community has not highlighted the subgraph perspective of these datasets; we purely treat them as datasets for graph prediction tasks. We can see that the above examples [2, 3] position their research as graph-level representation learning. These transformed datasets have been evaluated by many GNN models that perform graph prediction, surveying and comparing all of them is nearly impossible and beyond the scope of this paper.

Nevertheless, we accept these datasets as a line of related work targeting subgraph representations and will reflect them in the revision. Plus, we demonstrate the results of GCN and GAT as well-known baselines for performing graph-level prediction. We found that there is no significant performance difference between architectures.

|Model| FNTN| EM-User|HPO-Metab|
|-|-|-|-|
|GraphSAGE|84.9 ± 1.3|68.1 ± 2.6|44.1 ± 1.3|
|GCN|84.7 ± 1.5|72.8 ± 3.8|42.9 ± 1.9|
|GAT|85.1 ± 0.8|71.5 ± 5.7|43.1 ± 2.3|

[1] Deep graph infomax. ICLR 2019

[2] Graph Cross Networks with Vertex Infomax Pooling. NeurIPS 2020

[3] Graph Pooling via Coarsened Graph Infomax. SIGIR 2021

content.comment:
I don't think "Direct comparisons with various self-supervised models (including graphCL, GPT-GNN, and MVGRL mentioned by z3wS) are out of the scope of this paper."

Even if your setting is applied to full label setup, it's still a method that adds an auxiliary task to help better representation learning. To this end, these existing SSL methods are obviously valid baselines. For example, you take DGI as a baseline but neglect all the following-up works.
